output.title: The quiet cost of model deprecation
output.body:
If you are weighing automation against another hire, the part that gets missed is not the first build. It is what happens later if the model underneath the workflow changes, gets retired, or becomes too expensive to keep using.

For a small business, that can show up in ordinary work: customer-inquiry triage, lead qualification, or invoice handling. A workflow may look fine at launch and still need a decision later if the model version shifts or the vendor changes pricing. That is not a catastrophe; it is a maintenance choice, and it belongs in the business case up front.

The practical next step is simple: before you approve a pilot, ask one blunt question. If the underlying model is upgraded, retired, or repriced, does the workflow keep working, or do we need to rebuild it and pay again? If that answer is unclear, the plan is not finished yet.

If you include that question early, you compare automation and manual work more honestly. The cheapest entry price is not always the cheapest workflow.
